newsitem.title: FRANCE: French culture minister is anti-far right crusader.
newsitem.headline: French culture minister is anti-far right crusader.

text.p: Catherine Trautmann, named France's culture and communication minister on Wednesday, became a hero to the left in her picturesque power base of Strasbourg for leading a dogged resistance to the extreme-right National Front.

The 46-year-old Strasbourg mayor won national headlines -- and the emnity of Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen -- when she removed a statue of Joan of Arc, the anti-immigrant party's chief heroine, from the eastern city rather than let Le Pen use it as a prop during a party congress there in April.
Le Pen, in a typically theatrical display of his disdain for the Socialist mayor, later displayed a picture of her head perched on a platter at a campaign rally.

The daughter of a Protestant minister, Trautmann used her anti-Front activities to fuel her campaign for a National Assembly seat for Alsace, where voters generally give strong support to Le Pen despite the region's negligible immigrant population.

In addition to holding the culture and communication portfolios, she will also be spokesman for the new government of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, a post which will keep her in the public eye.

Her appointment marks her second stint as a cabinet minister. But her first, as senior citizens minister in 1988, ended after just a few weeks, when President Francois Mitterrand dissolved parliament and called new elections.

Trautmann's relations with Jospin have not always been the warmest. Due to her loyalty to ex-premier Michel Rocard, she was late to support Jospin in the 1995 presidential election, and several months went by before he campaigned in her fiefdom.
Born Catherine Argence in Strasbourg in 1951, she studied theology before entering Strasbourg's city council in 1983.

A disciple of Rocard's centre-left economic policies, Trautmann was practically unknown until 1986 when, under the proportional voting system in force at the time, she was elected to the National Assembly on a Socialist ticket.
She remained a deputy until 1988. A year later, she won Strasbourg's mayoral election and a seat in the Strasbourg-based European Parliament as well.
Her upset win over incumbent mayor Marcel Rudloff came as a surprise in a city that had voted centre-right for decades.

Evidently, Trautmann's energy and skill as an administrator were more important to voters than her wooden speaking style and her failure to master the local Alsatien dialect -- a first for a Strasbourg mayor.
France's only woman big-city mayor, she banned cars from the city centre to protect its Gothic cathedral -- Strasbourg's pride and joy -- from being eaten away by pollution.
Her idea of building a tramway, less expensive and quieter than a Metro, also was a great success and many cities have since followed suit.
In 1995, she was re-elected in the first round of municipal elections, little more than a month after 54 percent of Strasbourg's residents had voted for conservative Jacques Chirac for president.
